topic: High-Level Synthesis with Game Theoretic Scheduling

entries.objective: I identified five prior methods (ILP, LP, force-directed, simulated annealing, Sehwa) and their weaknesses from my reading. I wanted help formatting my comparison notes into a structured table for Section II.
entries.prompt: I have notes comparing five HLS scheduling/binding methods: ILP (exact, scheduling only, too complex), LP (exact, binding only), force-directed (heuristic, structural proxy not power), simulated annealing (stochastic, slow convergence), Sehwa (latency only, not power-aware), and game theory (auction/Nash, joint sched+binding, power-direct). Can you format this as a table with columns: Method, Type, Scope, Optimises power, Key limitation?
entries.ai_output_summary: Claude formatted my notes into the five-column comparison table with the correct entries for each method. It did not add any new methods or change any of my assessments. It also suggested adding 'Reference' as a column, which I declined since I preferred to cite in the row text.

actions: Verified each row against the corresponding reference. ILP/LP against Shiue and Chakrabarti [2], force-directed against Paulin and Knight [6], simulated annealing against Dasgupta and Karri [8], Sehwa against Park and Parker [8]. All characterisations match the papers. The game theory row is from my M1 analysis.

integration.section: Section II.A (Method Comparison Table, Table I)

entries.reflection: Every characterisation in the table came from my own reading of the references. The AI only converted my notes into table format. I adjusted the column headers and cell wording before including the table in the submission.

entries.objective: I wanted to explain in Section III why English and Dutch auctions do not fit the HLS binding problem and why second-price sealed-bid also does not fit. I had the reasoning in my notes but was not confident about the English auction terminology.
entries.prompt: In an English auction bids go up over time and in a Dutch auction bids go down over time. In second-price sealed-bid the winner pays the second-highest bid. For HLS binding where each unit has a fixed power cost that does not change during bidding, which of these three fits and which do not, and why?
entries.ai_output_summary: Claude confirmed my reasoning: English and Dutch auctions require dynamic bidding which conflicts with a fixed power-cost bid; second-price sealed-bid would mean the winning unit pays a cost it did not bid (the second-highest), which makes no physical sense when the cost is the actual power incurred; therefore first-price sealed-bid is the only appropriate type. The reasoning matched my notes exactly.

actions: Checked the auction selection argument against Murugavel and Ranganathan (2003) Section II and Owen (1995) [10]. The paper states that first-price sealed-bid is used. The exclusion reasoning for other types is my own logical argument, confirmed as sound by the AI but not explicitly stated in the paper.

issues: The exclusion reasoning for English, Dutch, and second-price auctions is my own argument and is not explicitly stated in Murugavel and Ranganathan. The AI confirmed the logic but this part of the text is my original reasoning, not sourced from the paper.

entries.reflection: The reasoning was mine; the AI acted as a sanity check. I included the exclusion argument in the submission as my own analytical contribution and noted in the text that the paper uses first-price sealed-bid without explicitly excluding other types.

entries.objective: I identified four tradeoff dimensions from my analysis: power vs. latency, power vs. area, solution quality vs. runtime, and scheduling-only vs. combined. I needed help structuring these into a summary table for Section IV.
entries.prompt: I have four tradeoffs for the game-theoretic HLS approach: (1) power vs. latency: power is primary, latency may increase up to 2 cycles; (2) power vs. area: no area overhead since no extra modules; (3) quality vs. runtime: Nash is NP-complete but small player count keeps it fast; (4) scheduling-only vs. combined: combined is better but more complex. Format this as a tradeoff summary table with columns: Dimension, Result, Note.
entries.ai_output_summary: Claude formatted my four tradeoffs into the three-column summary table. It also suggested a fifth row for 'Scalability' based on the NP-completeness point, which I accepted as it was already implied by my third tradeoff entry. No new tradeoff ideas were added that I had not already identified.

actions: Verified the quantitative values (power improvements 6-14%, latency increase up to 2 cycles, no area overhead) against Murugavel and Ranganathan (2003) Tables I-III and Section VI. All values are from the paper. The scalability note derives from Section V of the paper.

entries.reflection: All four tradeoff dimensions came from my analysis. The AI formatted them and suggested adding the scalability row, which was a logical extension of what I had already written. I included the scalability row and wrote all the cell content myself.
